204	published higher RC without matching selector advancement is an invalid,
205	fail-closed release state; it never authorizes resolution of the older cut as
206	the version-line latest.
207	
208	## Exact-Cut Qualification
209	
210	Qualification binds:
211	
212	- the Project Release Namespace, qualified immutable RC ref, annotated tag
213	  object, peeled commit, repository tree, Project Subtree root and tree, and
214	  declared Product member set;
215	- the exact release-scoped claim bytes;
216	- the governing Product and release basis;
217	- each claimed property and its observation boundary;
218	- evidence subjects, owner verdicts, and unresolved gaps; and
219	- the complete successor relation to the declared predecessor.
220	
221	Evidence matches the claim. Source success does not prove packaged or installed
222	behavior; packaging equivalence does not prove semantic behavior; artifact
223	presence does not prove usability unless presence is the exact claim.
224	
225	An RC is accepted only when the required exact-cut review and operator checks
226	are complete and the human authority accepts that exact subject. If review
227	requires any qualifying-byte change, the verdict remains attached to the old
228	RC and a higher RC is published. The selector already advertises the highest
229	published RC; acceptance does not move it, rewrite it, or create another final
230	carrier.
231	
232	## Monotonic Version-Line Advancement
233	
234	Version-line advancement makes the newly published highest RC for one Project
235	Release Namespace discoverable:
236	
237	1. identify the exact new immutable RC tag, ordinal, and peeled commit;
238	2. confirm that no higher RC ordinal already exists on that line;
239	3. confirm the project-qualified selector is absent or currently resolves to a
240	   lower RC ordinal on the same project line;
241	4. atomically create or force-update the annotated
242	   `<project>/v<version>` selector to the new highest RC commit;
243	5. create or update `release/<project>/<version>` to the same commit when that
244	   optional carrier is used;
245	6. push the carrier, RC branch, immutable RC tag, selector, and optional release
246	   branch atomically where the transport supports it; and
247	7. verify remotely that the selector peels to the highest RC commit and that
248	   the matching immutable annotated RC tag exists.
249	
250	Advancement is refused when the target has no matching immutable annotated RC
251	tag, any higher ordinal already exists, the selector would move to a lower RC,
252	or the selector and release branch would not align to the same highest commit.
253	
254	Forward movement is strictly monotonic by RC ordinal. A later defect is
255	repaired through a higher immutable RC, not by moving an old RC tag or rolling
256	the selector backward. The selector is therefore equivalent to
257	`v<version>-rc.latest`, while every concrete RC tag remains addressable.
258	
259	## Selector And Consumer Adoption
260	
261	The version-line selector answers only:
262	
263	> Which highest-ordinal published immutable RC cut currently exists on this
264	> version line?
265	
266	It never answers:
267	
268	> Which exact STDO cut governs this consumer?
269	
270	A Product Definition may retain `stdo://channels/<version>` as its discovery
271	selector, but its operative basis is the exact
272	`stdo://releases/v<version>-rc.<n>/` URI and installed-manifest digest. Moving
273	the Git version-line selector does not update any consumer. Adoption is a
274	separate explicit Product-Definition transition that resolves, presents,
275	installs, verifies, and pins the selected immutable RC. Resolution requires an
276	annotated selector with a distinct peeled commit; absence of a peeled selector
277	ref fails closed and cannot be interpreted as a lightweight selector whose tag
278	object is its commit.
279	
280	Channel resolution enumerates the published RC tags for the selected Project
281	Release Namespace, including preserved unqualified historical cuts during a
282	namespace transition, selects the greatest positive ordinal, requires that cut
283	and the current selector to be annotated tags peeling to the same commit, and
284	fails closed when the selector lags or points elsewhere. Channel adoption also
285	refuses a same-line target whose ordinal is below the Product Definition's
286	current exact basis. A consumer that intentionally retains an older cut names
287	that immutable RC URI and digest explicitly and uses exact-basis operations
288	such as `sync`; it does not express that choice through the latest-version
289	channel.
290	
291	Presentation and mutation are separate invocations. The read-only plan binds
292	the current Product Definition bytes and basis to the target immutable cut,
293	annotated tag object, peeled commit, tree, and installed-manifest digest, then
294	emits a deterministic plan digest. Mutation requires that exact digest as the
295	operator's acceptance and re-derives it before changing any Product Definition.
296	Selector, target, manifest, or definition drift invalidates the acceptance. A
297	fleet uses the same law with one aggregate digest over all exact per-definition
298	plans; planning inside a mutating invocation is not external presentation and
299	cannot authorize itself.
300	
301	This split lets operators refer to `v<version>` for the latest published RC
302	without repeatedly incrementing the version line, while every governed project
303	retains reproducible exact-cut authority and changes only through explicit
304	adoption.
305	
306	## Naming
307	
308	The shared-source naming shape is:
309	
310	- RC branch: `rc/<project>/<version>`;
311	- immutable RC tag: `<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>`;
312	- optional release branch: `release/<project>/<version>`; and
313	- mutable version-line selector tag: `<project>/v<version>`.
314	
315	For example:
316	
317	- candidate branch: `rc/stdo_representation/2.5.0`;
318	- first immutable cut: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0-rc.1`;
319	- second immutable cut: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0-rc.2`;
320	- latest-release branch: `release/stdo_representation/2.5.0`; and
321	- latest-published selector: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0`.
322	
323	The unqualified profile remains lawful only under the single-project and
324	historical-conservation conditions above. Projects may choose another spelling
325	only in a release source whose ref policy proves collision freedom and preserves
326	the same project namespace, mutable carrier, immutable cut, and mutable selector
327	distinctions.
328	
329	## Release-Scoped Assets
330	
331	An immutable RC cut may carry release-scoped surfaces such as:
332	
333	- release notes;
334	- release and installed-distribution manifests;
335	- dependency declarations;
336	- package or installed-carrier metadata;
337	- qualification receipts; and
338	- branch and tag identity declarations.
339	
340	Before RC publication, each used surface is reconciled to the exact RC subject.
341	After publication, changing one of those bytes creates a different candidate
342	and therefore requires a higher RC tag. The version-line selector has no
343	content-reconciliation phase because it adds no new Product bytes.
344	
345	Version-line branding does not belong in live present-tense Product or
346	requirements surfaces merely to signal recency. Exact version and RC identity
347	belong in release-scoped carriers and consumer basis bindings.
348	
349	## Coordinated Release-Matched Asset Cohorts
350	
351	A Product authority may declare an explicit cross-Product **Release-Matched
352	Asset Cohort** when one source corpus and its required distributed or derived
353	assets must remain usable as one versioned set. The declaring relation names
354	every required Product and asset, the exact source dependency, its owning
355	authorities, the qualification boundary, and the publication transaction. Path
356	co-location, equal version text, or a common actor cannot infer the relation.
357	
358	Every required member of one cohort uses one exact cohort version suffix
359	`<version>-rc.<n>`. Product-local cut names and refs render it as
360	`v<version>-rc.<n>`; embedded asset-version fields render the same suffix
361	without `v`. Qualification normalizes only that leading cut-name marker and
362	requires exact suffix equality. Equal versions establish release matching
363	only. They do not collapse Product identities, member inventories, tags,
364	acceptance judgments, or release authorities.
365	
366	For a release-matched STDO stack, the closed cohort contains all of:
367	
368	1. the exact STDO standards corpus cut;
369	2. the distributed `spec` plugin and host assets carried by that STDO cut;
370	3. the exact Axiom Indexer mechanics Product used to validate and project the
371	   index;
372	4. the exact STDO Representation Product; and
373	5. its released `a_c.STDO` axiomatic program and logical constraint map or
374	   equivalent semantic index, with the complete source-STDO member inventory,
375	   member digests, member-set digest, and exact cut identity used to derive it.
376	
377	The cohort is incomplete when a required member is missing, stale, differently
378	versioned, built from another source cut, or unable to reproduce its declared
379	source-member and digest closure. A change to any source member covered by the
380	index invalidates the old derived candidate for the successor cohort. The
381	index is regenerated, mechanically validated, independently qualified where
382	required, and released under the same new cut name. A stale index may remain
383	immutable history; it cannot accompany the changed source as the current
384	cohort.
385	
386	### Two-Commit Construction And One Publication Transaction
387	
388	Exact installed-manifest identity includes the annotated STDO tag object, so a
389	same-commit carrier containing both that identity and derived child bytes would
390	be self-referential. A coordinated STDO cohort therefore uses this bounded
391	two-commit construction:
392	
393	1. commit A freezes the exact STDO corpus, plugin, release record, and their
394	   qualification bytes;
395	2. the annotated STDO cut tag is created locally over commit A but is not
396	   pushed;
397	3. that exact local cut is installed and verified, producing the manifest
398	   identity used by every derived Product and index;
399	4. the Axiom Indexer, STDO Representation, semantic-index bytes, and cohort
400	   record are derived and frozen in commit B;
401	5. prepublication qualification evaluates commit B against the exact local
402	   STDO tag before child immutable tags are created;
403	6. annotated child cut tags and every Product-local RC branch, version-line
404	   selector, and optional release branch are prepared locally; and
405	7. a mandatory post-tag, pre-push gate re-runs qualification over every local
406	   annotated tag object and peel, selector, RC and release branch, normalized
407	   version mapping, target commit, and the exact closed ref set; it also fetches
408	   and binds the expected remote object ID or required absence for every
409	   destination ref; and
410	8. one transport transaction atomically publishes only that qualified carrier
411	   branch and
412	   complete Product ref set.
413	
414	If the remote does not support atomic ref publication, publication refuses.
415	The process has no sequential-push fallback. Every immutable cut tag is
416	create-only and therefore requires bound remote absence. Every mutable carrier,
417	RC branch, selector, and release branch uses an explicit per-ref
418	compare-and-swap lease, such as `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected-oid>`, in
419	that same atomic transaction. A missing expected ref, unexpected existing tag,
420	or changed remote object ID stops publication; the operator refetches and
421	repeats complete content and local-ref-graph qualification before constructing
422	another push. A lease mismatch never falls back to an unguarded force, a
423	partial push, or an in-place expectation update.
424	
425	Remote verification fails closed when any required cohort ref is absent,
426	lightweight, differently versioned, points to the wrong Product commit, or has
427	a selector or release branch that does not match its immutable cut.
428	Post-publication bookkeeping may use a later commit, but it cannot move any
429	immutable cohort tag.
430	
431	### Qualification And Recovery
432	
433	Prepublication content qualification binds the exact commit-A STDO tag and
434	manifest, commit-B source tree, all Product-local target refs, version markers,
435	Product member inventories, semantic-index bytes, and complete source-corpus
436	digest closure. It proves that the frozen candidate can be tagged without
437	changing a qualifying byte. After tag and mutable ref creation, local-ref-graph
438	qualification binds their annotated objects, peels, target commits, exact push
439	set, and every fetched remote expected object ID or required absence to that
440	unchanged content result. Post-publication qualification
441	verifies the same relation from remote refs and refuses a partial cohort.
442	
443	A historically published source cut may be the basis of a later same-version
444	backfill only when separately authorized recovery law names that exception.
445	Every recovered asset still binds the exact historical cut and same cut name,
446	and remote completeness remains mandatory. Recovery cannot move the historical
447	tag, add bytes to its Product subject, or be represented as an atomic cohort
448	that existed at the original publication. Normal successor publication uses
449	the atomic cohort process above.
450	
451	Adding or changing this cohort law changes qualifying Release Method bytes. It
452	governs only a higher immutable RC that contains those bytes and cannot
453	retroactively make an earlier cut a coordinated cohort.
454	
455	## Product Subject And Repository Carrier
456	
457	Before qualification, the project declares:
458	
459	- its Project Release Namespace and exact Project Subtree root;
460	- the exact Product member set or artifact constituting the release subject;
461	- the release-scoped claim surfaces describing that subject; and
462	- co-located mutable source-project fields excluded from both.
463	
464	A repository commit carries those declared sets but does not make every
465	co-located file or sibling Project Subtree a Product member. The exact
466	Project Subtree tree and Product member inventory distinguish the subject from
467	the wider carrier. Once the immutable RC is published, no post-review carrier
468	delta is admitted into that cut. Publication-caused ticket or source-work
469	bookkeeping is recorded afterward on the continuing source branch and cannot
470	move the immutable RC tag.
471	
472	## Acceptance Criteria
473	
474	An RC may be accepted when:
475	
476	- pre-RC qualification passed for the declared subject;
477	- independent exact-cut review passed where required;
478	- required operator review is complete;
479	- the intended release scope and successor relation are stable;
480	- release-scoped assets accurately describe the exact cut;
481	- all release-blocking gaps are closed or the claimed scope is explicitly
482	  narrowed; and
483	- the human Product authority accepted the exact immutable RC identity.
484	
485	Acceptance attaches to that immutable RC identity. It neither advances nor
486	rolls back the version-line selector. Consumer adoption separately evaluates
487	the exact latest target presented by the channel and mutates only after its
488	digest-bound plan is accepted.
489	
490	## External Qualification Dependencies
491	
492	Some claims depend on external backends, transports, or operator-facing
493	services outside the local carrier. Such a dependency may remain out of Product
494	for carrier and migration classification while still blocking the dependent
495	release claim.
496	
497	A clean skip caused by an unhealthy external dependency may preserve correct
498	Product classification, but it cannot establish that the dependent capability
499	passed. The claim is either qualified against a healthy dependency or narrowed
500	before acceptance.
501	
502	## Successor Baseline Conservation (`STDO-UP-015`)
503	
504	A successor identifies the exact predecessor immutable RC whose semantic claims
505	it evolves. That origin remains immutable for the candidate. Every predecessor
506	claim capable of affecting the successor receives one semantic disposition:
507	
508	- **conserved** — the successor retains the claim;
509	- **superseded** — an accepted successor relation replaces it;
510	- **intentionally removed** — current Product authority removes it; or
511	- **not applicable** — it has no successor effect, with a bounded reason.
512	
513	An unresolved disposition blocks qualification of the affected claim.
514	Conservation is semantic: patch absence does not prove loss when a
515	successor-native realization preserves behavior, and naming or code similarity
516	does not prove conservation without relevant evidence.
517	
518	Where a maintenance or support line may affect retained claims, the release
519	basis identifies the watched source, observation boundary, inclusion policy,
520	and successor candidate. Relevant changes receive semantic disposition at
521	material integration and exact-cut qualification. The consumer owns its record,
522	branch strategy, comparison, and proof mechanism.
523	
524	## Open Questions
525	
526	- What exact qualification bundle is mandatory for each Product class?
527	- What version-line compatibility rule requires a new `<version>` rather than a
528	  higher RC ordinal?
529

# Release Method

## Release-Publication Context

`RELEASE_METHOD.md` owns the release-publication bounded context
`urn:stdo:bounded-context:release-publication` under the selected complete STDO
basis. It owns the identities and transitions used to qualify, publish, and
select released cuts. It does not own Product meaning or consumer adoption.

## Position

Release process is distinct from live project specification.

Live specification defines the current constitutional truth of the project.
Release process defines how one published point-in-time cut is evaluated,
bounded, named, published, and made discoverable.

The product-local cut name is always:

```text
v<version>-rc.<n>
```

In a release source carrying one independently released project, that name may
also be the Git tag name. In a shared release source it is the suffix of the
project-qualified Git ref defined below. Equal product-local cut names do not
collapse releases owned by different projects.

The product-local version-line selector name is:

```text
v<version>
```

It denotes a mutable **Version-Line Selector**. The selector points to the
latest published immutable RC cut on that line, where latest means the greatest
positive RC ordinal published for that project and version line. It is
convenient discovery, not immutable identity and not sufficient as an exact
constitutional, dependency, evidence, or replay basis.

Release handling is downstream of intake triage. A bug, feature, regression,
or release blocker first receives its change class, lawful re-entry point,
affected scope, downstream proof obligations, and version-line disposition.
The existence of an RC window does not authorize untriaged mutation.

## Release Identities

The release-publication context distinguishes:

- **Project Release Namespace** — a stable repository-local key assigned by the
  Product release authority to one independently released source project;
- **Project Subtree** — the exact repository-relative source-project root and
  Git tree object selected for one cut;
- **Candidate Source** — mutable source-project state constructing a possible
  successor;
- **RC Branch** — a mutable project-qualified carrier for the current candidate
  window;
- **Immutable RC Cut** — an annotated project-qualified Git tag plus its exact
  Product release subject, naming one published candidate and, once accepted,
  one released Product;
- **Version-Line Selector** — the mutable project-qualified tag alias naming
  the highest-ordinal published immutable RC cut for that project and version
  line; and
- **Release Branch** — an optional mutable project-qualified convenience
  carrier aligned to the same latest-published commit as the selector.

Equal version text does not collapse these identities. Branches and the
version-line selector may move. An immutable RC tag never moves.

## Project-Qualified Git Refs

`<project>` is one explicit Project Release Namespace. It matches
`[a-z0-9]+(?:[-_][a-z0-9]+)*`, contains no slash, is unique within the release
source, and remains stable for the continuing release line. It is assigned by
the Product release authority. A directory name, display name, definition
label, package name, or matching version cannot infer or reassign it.

A shared release source uses these exact ref shapes for every future
publication:

```text
RC branch:              refs/heads/rc/<project>/<version>
immutable RC cut tag:   refs/tags/<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>
version-line selector:  refs/tags/<project>/v<version>
release branch:         refs/heads/release/<project>/<version>
```

The short Git tag names are therefore `<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>` and
`<project>/v<version>`. A shared release source must not publish a future cut or
selector under the unqualified `v<version>-rc.<n>` or `v<version>` refs.

A single-project release source may retain the unqualified ref profile only
while it has exactly one independently released project and its release record
declares that profile. Adding a second independently released project requires
project-qualified refs before either project publishes another cut.

For the Specification Stack shared source, the allocated namespaces are
`specification_methodology`, `axiom_indexer`, and `stdo_representation`. These
keys distinguish release refs; they do not merge the three Products or imply a
dependency or composition relation.

## Project-Subtree Release Identity

In a shared release source, an immutable cut binds all of:

- the Project Release Namespace and owning Product authority;
- the exact qualified Git ref and annotated tag object;
- the peeled commit and repository-root tree;
- the normalized repository-relative Project Subtree root at that commit;
- the Git tree object at that exact Project Subtree root;
- the declared Product member inventory and release-scoped claim bytes; and
- the predecessor and successor dispositions required by this method.

The Project Subtree root is a locator inside the exact peeled commit, not
Product identity. Its canonical spelling is the slash-separated Git path from
the repository root, with no leading or trailing slash and no empty, `.`, or
`..` component; `.` alone denotes the repository root. Each non-root component
must name the exact tree entry bytes traversed at that commit. Moving a source
project changes this locator and its cut identity without reassigning the
Project Release Namespace. If the source project occupies the repository root,
its project-subtree tree equals the repository-root tree.

A tag over a monorepo commit does not make sibling subtrees Product members.
Unrelated sibling bytes remain carrier state outside the declared Product
subject. Conversely, a member inventory or payload digest without the
qualified ref, commit, Project Subtree root, and Project Subtree tree is not a
complete reacquirable release identity.

## Historical Ref And Public-URI Conservation

Project qualification is prospective. Existing unqualified refs retain their
names, objects, peels, and public links. A historical tag object may remain
reachable through an additional archival ref, but it is not recreated,
re-annotated, moved, or replaced. An immutable historical tag remains the same
object regardless of which preserving ref reaches it.

Product-local cut names and public logical release URIs also remain unchanged.
In particular, a logical STDO release remains
`stdo://releases/v<version>-rc.<n>/`; the project-qualified Git ref is transport
identity and is not inserted into that URI. Resolution binds the public logical
cut to its exact historical or project-qualified Git ref and fails closed if
one project-local coordinate names different tag objects.

When one version line spans the transition, latest means the greatest positive
RC ordinal across that project's preserved historical cuts and its qualified
future cuts. The first qualified publication creates the qualified selector.
The historical unqualified selector is preserved at its existing object and
ceases to be the current selector for the shared source; it is not force-moved
to imitate the qualified namespace.

## Phases

The release process has three phases:

1. mutable candidate construction;
2. immutable RC publication and monotonic version-line advancement; and
3. exact-cut qualification, acceptance, and explicit consumer adoption.

There is no second final cut after an accepted RC. Publication immediately
makes the new highest ordinal discoverable through the version-line selector;
acceptance remains a verdict over the exact immutable RC rather than a second
carrier. If any byte capable of affecting the Product or a release-scoped claim
changes, the project publishes and reviews a higher immutable RC cut instead.

## Mutable Candidate Construction

During candidate construction:

- bounded fixes are allowed after intake triage;
- qualification and operator review may continue;
- release notes may remain draft until RC publication;
- the RC branch may move; and
- mutable source is explicitly non-operative for released consumers.

The intended Product boundary, release-scoped claims, excluded source-project
state, and qualification basis become explicit before RC publication. A
material scope change is repriced instead of being silently absorbed.

## Immutable RC Publication

A published RC cut exists to provide one exact subject for review, replay, and
possible acceptance. To publish it, the project:

1. confirms the triaged scope and lawful constitutional re-entry;
2. declares the exact Product release subject and release-scoped claim set;
3. reconciles the release note and other release-facing assets to that subject;
4. runs the proportionate pre-RC qualification and operator checks;
5. commits the exact carrier;
6. resolves and records the exact Project Release Namespace, Project Subtree
   root, and Project Subtree tree;
7. creates one annotated immutable `<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>` tag and an
   annotated `<project>/v<version>` selector tag over that same commit in a
   shared release source;
8. atomically pushes the carrier, RC branch, immutable RC tag, selector, and
   optional release branch where the transport supports it;
9. verifies remotely that the immutable tag, selector, and release branch
   resolve to the highest published RC commit; and
10. records enough ref, subtree, identity, and inventory evidence to reacquire
    the cut without trusting a mutable checkout.

Each published RC tag is immutable. Further work increments `<n>` on the same
version line when the intended line remains applicable. It does not require a
minor-version increment merely because review found a bounded repair. A
published higher RC without matching selector advancement is an invalid,
fail-closed release state; it never authorizes resolution of the older cut as
the version-line latest.

## Exact-Cut Qualification

Qualification binds:

- the Project Release Namespace, qualified immutable RC ref, annotated tag
  object, peeled commit, repository tree, Project Subtree root and tree, and
  declared Product member set;
- the exact release-scoped claim bytes;
- the governing Product and release basis;
- each claimed property and its observation boundary;
- evidence subjects, owner verdicts, and unresolved gaps; and
- the complete successor relation to the declared predecessor.

Evidence matches the claim. Source success does not prove packaged or installed
behavior; packaging equivalence does not prove semantic behavior; artifact
presence does not prove usability unless presence is the exact claim.

An RC is accepted only when the required exact-cut review and operator checks
are complete and the human authority accepts that exact subject. If review
requires any qualifying-byte change, the verdict remains attached to the old
RC and a higher RC is published. The selector already advertises the highest
published RC; acceptance does not move it, rewrite it, or create another final
carrier.

## Monotonic Version-Line Advancement

Version-line advancement makes the newly published highest RC for one Project
Release Namespace discoverable:

1. identify the exact new immutable RC tag, ordinal, and peeled commit;
2. confirm that no higher RC ordinal already exists on that line;
3. confirm the project-qualified selector is absent or currently resolves to a
   lower RC ordinal on the same project line;
4. atomically create or force-update the annotated
   `<project>/v<version>` selector to the new highest RC commit;
5. create or update `release/<project>/<version>` to the same commit when that
   optional carrier is used;
6. push the carrier, RC branch, immutable RC tag, selector, and optional release
   branch atomically where the transport supports it; and
7. verify remotely that the selector peels to the highest RC commit and that
   the matching immutable annotated RC tag exists.

Advancement is refused when the target has no matching immutable annotated RC
tag, any higher ordinal already exists, the selector would move to a lower RC,
or the selector and release branch would not align to the same highest commit.

Forward movement is strictly monotonic by RC ordinal. A later defect is
repaired through a higher immutable RC, not by moving an old RC tag or rolling
the selector backward. The selector is therefore equivalent to
`v<version>-rc.latest`, while every concrete RC tag remains addressable.

## Selector And Consumer Adoption

The version-line selector answers only:

> Which highest-ordinal published immutable RC cut currently exists on this
> version line?

It never answers:

> Which exact STDO cut governs this consumer?

A Product Definition may retain `stdo://channels/<version>` as its discovery
selector, but its operative basis is the exact
`stdo://releases/v<version>-rc.<n>/` URI and installed-manifest digest. Moving
the Git version-line selector does not update any consumer. Adoption is a
separate explicit Product-Definition transition that resolves, presents,
installs, verifies, and pins the selected immutable RC. Resolution requires an
annotated selector with a distinct peeled commit; absence of a peeled selector
ref fails closed and cannot be interpreted as a lightweight selector whose tag
object is its commit.

Channel resolution enumerates the published RC tags for the selected Project
Release Namespace, including preserved unqualified historical cuts during a
namespace transition, selects the greatest positive ordinal, requires that cut
and the current selector to be annotated tags peeling to the same commit, and
fails closed when the selector lags or points elsewhere. Channel adoption also
refuses a same-line target whose ordinal is below the Product Definition's
current exact basis. A consumer that intentionally retains an older cut names
that immutable RC URI and digest explicitly and uses exact-basis operations
such as `sync`; it does not express that choice through the latest-version
channel.

Presentation and mutation are separate invocations. The read-only plan binds
the current Product Definition bytes and basis to the target immutable cut,
annotated tag object, peeled commit, tree, and installed-manifest digest, then
emits a deterministic plan digest. Mutation requires that exact digest as the
operator's acceptance and re-derives it before changing any Product Definition.
Selector, target, manifest, or definition drift invalidates the acceptance. A
fleet uses the same law with one aggregate digest over all exact per-definition
plans; planning inside a mutating invocation is not external presentation and
cannot authorize itself.

This split lets operators refer to `v<version>` for the latest published RC
without repeatedly incrementing the version line, while every governed project
retains reproducible exact-cut authority and changes only through explicit
adoption.

## Naming

The shared-source naming shape is:

- RC branch: `rc/<project>/<version>`;
- immutable RC tag: `<project>/v<version>-rc.<n>`;
- optional release branch: `release/<project>/<version>`; and
- mutable version-line selector tag: `<project>/v<version>`.

For example:

- candidate branch: `rc/stdo_representation/2.5.0`;
- first immutable cut: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0-rc.1`;
- second immutable cut: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0-rc.2`;
- latest-release branch: `release/stdo_representation/2.5.0`; and
- latest-published selector: `stdo_representation/v2.5.0`.

The unqualified profile remains lawful only under the single-project and
historical-conservation conditions above. Projects may choose another spelling
only in a release source whose ref policy proves collision freedom and preserves
the same project namespace, mutable carrier, immutable cut, and mutable selector
distinctions.

## Release-Scoped Assets

An immutable RC cut may carry release-scoped surfaces such as:

- release notes;
- release and installed-distribution manifests;
- dependency declarations;
- package or installed-carrier metadata;
- qualification receipts; and
- branch and tag identity declarations.

Before RC publication, each used surface is reconciled to the exact RC subject.
After publication, changing one of those bytes creates a different candidate
and therefore requires a higher RC tag. The version-line selector has no
content-reconciliation phase because it adds no new Product bytes.

Version-line branding does not belong in live present-tense Product or
requirements surfaces merely to signal recency. Exact version and RC identity
belong in release-scoped carriers and consumer basis bindings.

## Coordinated Release-Matched Asset Cohorts

A Product authority may declare an explicit cross-Product **Release-Matched
Asset Cohort** when one source corpus and its required distributed or derived
assets must remain usable as one versioned set. The declaring relation names
every required Product and asset, the exact source dependency, its owning
authorities, the qualification boundary, and the publication transaction. Path
co-location, equal version text, or a common actor cannot infer the relation.

Every required member of one cohort uses one exact cohort version suffix
`<version>-rc.<n>`. Product-local cut names and refs render it as
`v<version>-rc.<n>`; embedded asset-version fields render the same suffix
without `v`. Qualification normalizes only that leading cut-name marker and
requires exact suffix equality. Equal versions establish release matching
only. They do not collapse Product identities, member inventories, tags,
acceptance judgments, or release authorities.

For a release-matched STDO stack, the closed cohort contains all of:

1. the exact STDO standards corpus cut;
2. the distributed `spec` plugin and host assets carried by that STDO cut;
3. the exact Axiom Indexer mechanics Product used to validate and project the
   index;
4. the exact STDO Representation Product; and
5. its released `a_c.STDO` axiomatic program and logical constraint map or
   equivalent semantic index, with the complete source-STDO member inventory,
   member digests, member-set digest, and exact cut identity used to derive it.

The cohort is incomplete when a required member is missing, stale, differently
versioned, built from another source cut, or unable to reproduce its declared
source-member and digest closure. A change to any source member covered by the
index invalidates the old derived candidate for the successor cohort. The
index is regenerated, mechanically validated, independently qualified where
required, and released under the same new cut name. A stale index may remain
immutable history; it cannot accompany the changed source as the current
cohort.

### Two-Commit Construction And One Publication Transaction

Exact installed-manifest identity includes the annotated STDO tag object, so a
same-commit carrier containing both that identity and derived child bytes would
be self-referential. A coordinated STDO cohort therefore uses this bounded
two-commit construction:

1. commit A freezes the exact STDO corpus, plugin, release record, and their
   qualification bytes;
2. the annotated STDO cut tag is created locally over commit A but is not
   pushed;
3. that exact local cut is installed and verified, producing the manifest
   identity used by every derived Product and index;
4. the Axiom Indexer, STDO Representation, semantic-index bytes, and cohort
   record are derived and frozen in commit B;
5. prepublication qualification evaluates commit B against the exact local
   STDO tag before child immutable tags are created;
6. annotated child cut tags and every Product-local RC branch, version-line
   selector, and optional release branch are prepared locally; and
7. a mandatory post-tag, pre-push gate re-runs qualification over every local
   annotated tag object and peel, selector, RC and release branch, normalized
   version mapping, target commit, and the exact closed ref set; it also fetches
   and binds the expected remote object ID or required absence for every
   destination ref; and
8. one transport transaction atomically publishes only that qualified carrier
   branch and
   complete Product ref set.

If the remote does not support atomic ref publication, publication refuses.
The process has no sequential-push fallback. Every immutable cut tag is
create-only and therefore requires bound remote absence. Every mutable carrier,
RC branch, selector, and release branch uses an explicit per-ref
compare-and-swap lease, such as `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected-oid>`, in
that same atomic transaction. A missing expected ref, unexpected existing tag,
or changed remote object ID stops publication; the operator refetches and
repeats complete content and local-ref-graph qualification before constructing
another push. A lease mismatch never falls back to an unguarded force, a
partial push, or an in-place expectation update.

Remote verification fails closed when any required cohort ref is absent,
lightweight, differently versioned, points to the wrong Product commit, or has
a selector or release branch that does not match its immutable cut.
Post-publication bookkeeping may use a later commit, but it cannot move any
immutable cohort tag.

### Qualification And Recovery

Prepublication content qualification binds the exact commit-A STDO tag and
manifest, commit-B source tree, all Product-local target refs, version markers,
Product member inventories, semantic-index bytes, and complete source-corpus
digest closure. It proves that the frozen candidate can be tagged without
changing a qualifying byte. After tag and mutable ref creation, local-ref-graph
qualification binds their annotated objects, peels, target commits, exact push
set, and every fetched remote expected object ID or required absence to that
unchanged content result. Post-publication qualification
verifies the same relation from remote refs and refuses a partial cohort.

A historically published source cut may be the basis of a later same-version
backfill only when separately authorized recovery law names that exception.
Every recovered asset still binds the exact historical cut and same cut name,
and remote completeness remains mandatory. Recovery cannot move the historical
tag, add bytes to its Product subject, or be represented as an atomic cohort
that existed at the original publication. Normal successor publication uses
the atomic cohort process above.

Adding or changing this cohort law changes qualifying Release Method bytes. It
governs only a higher immutable RC that contains those bytes and cannot
retroactively make an earlier cut a coordinated cohort.

## Product Subject And Repository Carrier

Before qualification, the project declares:

- its Project Release Namespace and exact Project Subtree root;
- the exact Product member set or artifact constituting the release subject;
- the release-scoped claim surfaces describing that subject; and
- co-located mutable source-project fields excluded from both.

A repository commit carries those declared sets but does not make every
co-located file or sibling Project Subtree a Product member. The exact
Project Subtree tree and Product member inventory distinguish the subject from
the wider carrier. Once the immutable RC is published, no post-review carrier
delta is admitted into that cut. Publication-caused ticket or source-work
bookkeeping is recorded afterward on the continuing source branch and cannot
move the immutable RC tag.

## Acceptance Criteria

An RC may be accepted when:

- pre-RC qualification passed for the declared subject;
- independent exact-cut review passed where required;
- required operator review is complete;
- the intended release scope and successor relation are stable;
- release-scoped assets accurately describe the exact cut;
- all release-blocking gaps are closed or the claimed scope is explicitly
  narrowed; and
- the human Product authority accepted the exact immutable RC identity.

Acceptance attaches to that immutable RC identity. It neither advances nor
rolls back the version-line selector. Consumer adoption separately evaluates
the exact latest target presented by the channel and mutates only after its
digest-bound plan is accepted.

## External Qualification Dependencies

Some claims depend on external backends, transports, or operator-facing
services outside the local carrier. Such a dependency may remain out of Product
for carrier and migration classification while still blocking the dependent
release claim.

A clean skip caused by an unhealthy external dependency may preserve correct
Product classification, but it cannot establish that the dependent capability
passed. The claim is either qualified against a healthy dependency or narrowed
before acceptance.

## Successor Baseline Conservation (`STDO-UP-015`)

A successor identifies the exact predecessor immutable RC whose semantic claims
it evolves. That origin remains immutable for the candidate. Every predecessor
claim capable of affecting the successor receives one semantic disposition:

- **conserved** — the successor retains the claim;
- **superseded** — an accepted successor relation replaces it;
- **intentionally removed** — current Product authority removes it; or
- **not applicable** — it has no successor effect, with a bounded reason.

An unresolved disposition blocks qualification of the affected claim.
Conservation is semantic: patch absence does not prove loss when a
successor-native realization preserves behavior, and naming or code similarity
does not prove conservation without relevant evidence.

Where a maintenance or support line may affect retained claims, the release
basis identifies the watched source, observation boundary, inclusion policy,
and successor candidate. Relevant changes receive semantic disposition at
material integration and exact-cut qualification. The consumer owns its record,
branch strategy, comparison, and proof mechanism.

## Open Questions

- What exact qualification bundle is mandatory for each Product class?
- What version-line compatibility rule requires a new `<version>` rather than a
  higher RC ordinal?

43	
44	## Position
45	
46	Spec-driven development treats specification as constitutional source, not as
47	commentary on code after the fact.
48	
49	The point is to make software re-derivable, auditable, and correctable under
50	explicit authority.
51	
52	Its overriding bias is declarative rather than imperative.
53	
54	In the age of LLMs, the system should primarily declare truths, structures,
55	interfaces, constraints, and evidence surfaces, then let lawful processing
56	derive and realize work from that declared surface.
57	
58	Imperative procedure still exists, but it is subordinate to declared authority.
59	
60	---
61	
62	## STDO Method Identity
63	
64	`SPEC_METHOD.md` owns the method-identity bounded context
65	`urn:stdo:bounded-context:method-identity` under the selected complete STDO
66	basis.
67	
68	Within that context, **STDO** is the shorthand for the method's four key
69	pillars:
70	
71	- **S** — Specification, owned by `SPEC_METHOD.md`;
72	- **T** — Ticketing, owned by `TICKET_METHOD.md`;
73	- **D** — Design, owned by `DESIGN_MODULE_METHOD.md`; and
74	- **O** — Outcome-Driven Development, owned by `ODD_METHOD.md`.
75	
76	The `O` names the complete Outcome-Driven Development pillar. `ODD_METHOD.md`
77	owns the `ODD` identity and graph-native meaning. This expansion does not make
78	the four named files independently selectable or reduce the STDO Product to
79	four members. Consumer authority remains one complete immutable released STDO
80	cut with its exact member inventory.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## Probabilistic Work Boundary
85	
86	Spec-driven development exists to govern the boundary around work, not to absorb
87	the worker's internal solution strategy into the framework.
88	
89	For any probabilistic, agentic, or delegated work unit, the live specification
90	and design should declare:
91	
92	- the input and output contract
93	- the required context
94	- the capability or role expectation
95	- the admissible evidence and evaluator regime
96	- the provenance obligation
97	- the lawful stop, hold, gap, continuation, or completion states
98	
99	The worker, tool, agent, or domain implementation owns the internal HOW inside
100	that declared boundary unless the product explicitly promotes part of that HOW
101	into reusable declared structure.
102	
103	Deterministic checks and validation are evidence surfaces. They may optimize or
104	prove a domain-local path where the domain can make part of the work precise.
105	They do not authorize the methodology, runtime, or framework to absorb domain
106	solution strategy as constitutional law.
107	
108	In graph-native refinements such as `ODD_METHOD.md`, this boundary is usually
109	one vector or edge traversal. The traversal is the admissible external space.
110	Any unconstrained part of a probabilistic worker's reasoning remains hidden
111	worker-internal traversal and must be forced back through declared contracts,
112	evidence, provenance, and control truth.
113	
114	If a framework layer begins prescribing domain solution strategy beyond the
115	declared work contract and control truth, it has crossed its authority boundary.

117	---
118	
119	## Recursive Product Taxonomy
120	
121	`SPEC_METHOD.md` owns this taxonomy in the recursive-product bounded context
122	`urn:stdo:bounded-context:recursive-product-taxonomy` under the selected
123	complete STDO basis.
124	
125	Software is recursive and compositional.
126	
127	A released product may be used to build:
128	
129	- the next released version of itself
130	- a dependent product
131	- downstream project artifacts
132	
133	Most taxonomy drift in recursive software systems comes from collapsing these
134	roles into one overloaded word such as `product`.
135	
136	This methodology therefore distinguishes:
137	
138	- **Substrate** (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:substrate`): a
139	  lower product or runtime used to build other products;
140	- **Development Product**
141	  (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:development-product`): the
142	  role of one exact Install of a released Product while that Install acts as
143	  builder substrate for a Source Project. The role creates no new Product
144	  identity and transfers no meaning or authority from the builder to the
145	  Product being authored;
146	- **Source Project**
147	  (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:source-project`): the mutable
148	  workspace building the next release cut;
149	- **Release Cut**
150	  (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:release-cut`): one immutable
151	  annotated RC boundary over a published feature set;
152	- **Product** (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:product`): the
153	  released immutable thing resulting when that release cut is accepted;
154	- **Install** (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:install`): a
155	  stamped workspace instance of that released product;
156	- **Artifact** (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:artifact`): any
157	  published output built by a source project or by a configured installed
158	  product; and
159	- **Product Definition**
160	  (`urn:stdo:concept:recursive-product-taxonomy:product-definition`): the
161	  present-tense source-project authority surface conventionally carried by
162	  `PRODUCT.md`; it defines the current product `WHAT` for decomposition and is
163	  not the released Product artifact.
164	
165	The governing rules are:
166	
167	- do not call a mutable source workspace a product
168	- when a released Product acts as builder substrate, bind the exact Install as
169	  a Development Product without confusing it with the Product being authored
170	- do not confuse an immutable RC release cut or installed product with the mutable source
171	  project building the next cut
172	- `PRODUCT.md` is the product-definition surface of a source project, not the
173	  released product artifact itself
174	- products may depend on other products
175	- installed products may build the next version of themselves or other products
176	
177	The compiler analogy is the intended model:
178	
179	`bootstrap source -> release P0 -> install P0 -> use P0 to build source for P1 -> release P1`
180	
181	This taxonomy is load-bearing.
182	
183	If it is blurred, dependency and self-hosting errors compound quickly and are
184	expensive to unwind.

188	## Manifesto
189	
190	We define the current **goals** for the active body of work before repricing deeper constitutional layers.
191	
192	We work from **intent** before implementation.
193	
194	We define the current **product definition** in explicit present-tense terms before decomposing it into detailed requirements.
195	
196	We define the full constitutional **what** in **requirements**, not merely a feature list.
197	
198	We prefer declaring desired truth and lawful boundaries over prescribing step-by-step imperative procedure.
199	
200	We make **design** the explicit structural bridge between requirements and code.
201	
202	We require **code** to be derivable from requirements and design, not defended as accidental precedent.
203	
204	We treat spec-driven development as a **disambiguation pipeline**: each major gate reduces the space of lawful interpretations before downstream realization proceeds.
205	
206	We demand **evidence** for claims through scenarios, tests, events, projection, and delta.
207	
208	We treat **repricing** as part of correctness: when reality exposes a constitutional gap, the specification must change.
209	
210	We keep **authority directional** even while iterating: goals govern intent, intent governs product definition, product definition governs requirements, requirements govern design, and requirements plus design govern code.
211	
212	We keep the **live operative surface** in the present tense only: once a new current reality is established, transitional paths are erased from the live product unless explicitly retained as compatibility features.
213	
214	We treat **derived artifacts** — indexes, trace matrices, reports, automation, generated views — as helpful read models, never as constitutional truth.
215	
216	If these claims do not hold, the work is not genuinely spec-driven.

220	## Spec-Drivenness Litmus
221	
222	The work is not genuinely spec-driven if any of these fail:
223	
224	1. Given goals, a competent team cannot derive a conformant intent surface.
225	2. Given intent, a competent team cannot derive a conformant product-definition surface.
226	3. Given product definition, a competent team cannot derive conformant requirements.
227	4. Given requirements, a competent team cannot derive a conformant design.
228	5. Given requirements and design, a competent team cannot derive conformant code.
229	6. A live requirement has no explicit status, category, or owning design decision.
230	7. A live requirement has no downstream realization or explicit deferment surface.
231	8. Code behavior exists without requirement and design authority.
232	9. A live domain artifact is rewritten in place after becoming part of the live constitutional surface.
233	10. A capability claim has no operational evidence.
234	11. Drift is discovered, but the constitutional source is not repriced.
235	12. A major ambiguity at a constitutional or realization boundary is neither recorded nor explicitly governed.
236	13. A material product, module, function, application, runtime surface, or
237	    capability has no declared operational lifecycle signal and no recorded
238	    gap for unanswered release, deployment, live-use, telemetry, or retirement
239	    questions.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Process Constitution
244	
245	This methodology is not only a local operating note for one implementation. It is the process constitution for building projects by spec-driven development.
246	
247	Its role is meta-constitutional:
248	
249	- it defines how goals, intent, product, requirements, design, code, evidence, and repricing relate
250	- it defines what counts as specification sufficiency
251	- it defines what kinds of requirement truth exist
252	- it defines how authority flows during iterative delivery
253	
254	Therefore, if a project's implementation disappears, this methodology should still be sufficient to bootstrap a new spec-driven project process from scratch.
255	
256	The important boundary is:
257	
258	- `SPEC_METHOD.md` defines the process constitution
259	- `GOALS.md` conventionally names the current overriding concerns for the active body of work
260	- `INTENT.md` conventionally names domain direction
261	- `PRODUCT.md` conventionally names the current product-definition surface of the mutable source project
262	- `specification/requirements/` is the conventional live requirement surface derived from product definition
263	- a shared design surface plus any tenant-local design surfaces choose the concrete mechanism
264	- the product's `stdo_<label>.json` definition binds the actual authority
265	  locations; these conventional names do not require an existing project to
266	  move or duplicate its files
267	- the definition's `how.build_tenants` entries locate the project-owned
268	  realizations beneath one shared specification
269	
270	The authoritative split is strict:
271	
272	- the surfaces bound by `what` define `WHAT`
273	- design and realization surfaces define `HOW`
274	- no build-tenant, design, code, definition overlay, or derived surface may
275	  become co-equal constitutional authority with the bound `WHAT`
276	
277	In the default scaffold, `requirements/` is a folder under `specification/`.
278	Requirements may instead be stored at any URI bound by the product definition,
279	as individual files or grouped into requirement families. The purpose of the
280	default shape is to avoid collapsing the constitutional surface into one
281	monolithic requirements document, not to make folder placement constitutional.
282	
283	This is one expression of the broader declarative bias: we prefer declaring requirement structure and family boundaries over maintaining one imperative catch-all document.
284	
285	So if project-specific design and code disappeared, recovery would proceed through this methodology plus the surviving domain specification. Methodology alone can bootstrap the process; methodology plus domain specification can reconstruct the project.
286	
287	---
288	
289	## STDO Product Definition Overlay And Layout Independence
290	
291	`SPEC_METHOD.md` owns the product-definition-routing bounded context
292	`urn:stdo:bounded-context:product-definition-routing` under the selected
293	complete STDO basis. This section defines that context's overlay, definition,
294	discovery, locator, and composition concepts. The JSON schema realizes its
295	accepted interoperability shape but does not become a second semantic owner.
296	
297	Every STDO-defined product publishes one JSON definition for each distinct
298	current product `WHAT`. Its conventional filename is:
299	
300	```text
301	stdo_<label>.json
302	```
303	
304	`stdo_default.json` is the default filename for a source project with one
305	product definition. A directory may contain more than one definition when it
306	hosts more than one distinct product `WHAT`. Multiple build tenants realizing
307	the same `WHAT` remain entries in one definition and do not create additional
308	definition files.
309	
310	The suffix `<label>` is the **Definition Label**: a stable lowercase local
311	discovery label made from ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, or underscores. It is
312	unique only among definitions in the same directory. It is not Product
313	identity. The `product.definition_id` URI inside the definition is the
314	**Product-Definition Identity**: the stable identity of the mutable
315	product-definition line, unique within the discovered workspace definition
316	set. It identifies one continuing `WHAT` definition, not one immutable released
317	Product.
318	
319	The definition identity may remain stable while that source line authors
320	successive Product releases. Every immutable Product or release produced from
321	the line retains its own Product- and Release-Method identity. A fork,
322	replacement, or independently governed `WHAT` definition receives another
323	`product.definition_id`; changing a released Product does not repurpose the
324	definition identity as release identity.
325	
326	Product-definition, immutable Product, bounded-context, and build-tenant
327	identity URIs are identity carriers, not self-authorizing strings. They remain
328	subject to `IDENTITY_METHOD.md` and the owning Product, release, or domain
329	authority. A URI locator, filename, path, or display label cannot mint or widen
330	identity authority.
331	
332	The directory containing a definition is its **definition root**. Relative URI
333	references resolve against the definition file's retrieval URI. The
334	`product.source_project` reference identifies the source-project root and may
335	resolve to the definition root or elsewhere. File proximity does not create
336	authority.
337	
338	The normative schema is
339	`schemas/product-definition.schema.json`. The single fill-in form is
340	`templates/PRODUCT_DEFINITION_TEMPLATE.json`. This concrete JSON shape is an
341	accepted interoperability boundary under `STDO-SURFACE-001`. It standardizes
342	only identity, location, relation, and discovery fields. It does not absorb the
343	meaning owned by any referenced constitutional, Product, requirement, design,
344	ticket, or commentary surface.
345	
346	### Required Definition Relations
347	
348	Each definition contains:
349	
350	- `product` — stable product-definition identity, display name, source-project
351	  locator, and an explicit bounded-context declaration or `null`;
352	- `constitution.stdo` — the STDO source repository, mutable version-line
353	  discovery selector, and exact installed release basis with its deterministic
354	  manifest digest;
355	- `constitution.additional_authorities` — every non-STDO constitutional set;
356	- `constitution.entrypoints` — basis-qualified useful reading routes; and
357	- `constitution.agent_bootstrap` — the constitutional entrypoint and
358	  marker-managed agent-instruction targets;
359	- `local_constitution` — local axioms, overrides, and disambiguations with
360	  their owning authority, target, basis, and scope, including context-qualified
361	  term resolution where applicable;
362	- `reference_frame_bases` — one or more accepted collective reference-frame
363	  basis declarations with their admitting authorities and governed scopes;
364	- `what` — the current Intent, Product, and specification bindings;
365	- `how` — any shared realization surfaces and one or more independent build
366	  tenants;
367	- `ticketing` — Goals, ticket, comment, and optional sprint carrier bindings;
368	- `composition` — explicit relations to other STDO product definitions; and
369	- `$schema` and `kind` — the schema locator and
370	  `stdo.product-definition` discriminator.
371	
372	The overlay owns this locator and relation map. Referenced documents own their
373	content. Repeating source truth inside the JSON creates a rival authority and
374	is non-conformant.
375	
376	`product.bounded_context` identifies the enclosing bounded context of the
377	definition's own product `WHAT`, or is `null` when no separate enclosing context
378	is claimed. It is not an exhaustive registry and does not flatten subordinate,
379	peer, composed, tenant, user, or runtime contexts into one namespace. Those
380	contexts remain defined by their owning authorities; every local
381	disambiguation names the exact context in which its resolution applies.
382	
383	### Constitutional-Set Sufficiency
384	
385	A **Constitutional Set** is the complete set of governing documents selected
386	for a product, not five prescribed files. Collectively, the selected set must
387	make the following recoverable for the governed scope:
388	
389	- **axioms** — irreducible starting truths, invariants, and refusal conditions;
390	- **ontology** — the kinds of things treated as real and their material
391	  identities, relations, boundaries, and lifecycle;
392	- **epistemology** — how claims become knowable or acceptable, including
393	  admissible evidence, observation, uncertainty, falsification, and decision
394	  authority;
395	- **taxonomy** — the classifications and kind distinctions used to prevent
396	  category collapse; and
397	- **semantics** — the governed meaning of terms, relations, states, operations,
398	  and outcomes.
399

586	### Bounded-Context Semantic Resolution
587	
588	`SPEC_METHOD.md` owns this law in the semantic-resolution bounded context
589	`urn:stdo:bounded-context:semantic-resolution` under the selected complete STDO
590	basis. The glossary may index this identity but does not participate in its
591	declaration.
592	
593	A **term** is a lexical label used in an occurrence, not a context-free concept
594	identity. A **bounded context** is an explicitly identified semantic scope in
595	which a governed vocabulary, concept set, and relation set are jointly
596	interpretable under named authority. A **concept reference** is an exact,
597	resolvable reference to a meaning owned by an authority under a selected basis;
598	the reference locates that meaning but does not mint it or its authority.
599	
600	A bounded context exists only when an owning authority declares its stable
601	identity, owner, selected basis, and governed semantic scope. A consuming
602	standard may define a concept inside that context only through an explicit
603	owner relation. A filename, heading, index row, glossary section, schema value,
604	or bare URI cannot constitute the context.
605	
606	Every material term occurrence resolves under this **semantic address**:
607	
608	```text
609	(term, bounded-context identity, owning authority, selected basis, governed scope)
610	```
611	
612	Equal spelling, capitalization, shape, file location, directory nesting, actor,
613	or implementation does not establish equal meaning, concept identity,
614	equivalence, inheritance, or authority. Different spelling also does not prove
615	different meaning. Those relations follow only from the applicable semantic
616	address or an explicit authorized relation.
617	
618	Resolution proceeds in this order:
619	
620	1. identify the occurrence's governed scope and nearest explicit bounded-
621	   context declaration;
622	2. identify the exact selected basis and the authorities applicable to that
623	   context and scope;
624	3. collect context-local definitions and explicitly imported concept
625	   references admitted by those authorities and that basis;
626	4. apply every applicable owner-authorized override or disambiguation; and
627	5. admit the occurrence only when exactly one concept remains.
628	
629	A document, section, schema field, operation, or other owning surface may
630	declare a context for all subordinate occurrences, so uniquely resolved prose
631	does not need to repeat a qualifier on every term. A repository, directory,
632	filename, heading, glossary match, prompt, actor, or nearby definition does not
633	declare a bounded context by accident.
634	
635	Zero applicable concepts is unresolved meaning. More than one is ambiguous
636	meaning. Both fail closed at a material boundary: an agent, design, schema,
637	implementation, test, translation, or reviewer must not select one by
638	familiarity, frequency, recency, nominal match, or a context-free glossary
639	fallback.
640	
641	`GLOSSARY_GUIDE.md` is a non-deciding locator index. Each record points to an
642	exact source clause that declares the bounded context and owns the indexed
643	concept. The glossary defines neither and cannot repair a missing declaration.
644	An indexed concept is applicable only when the semantic address selects its
645	owning clause or the target context explicitly imports it; appearance in the
646	glossary creates no shared default.
647	
648	A cross-context relation is explicit and owner-authorized. Its carrier states:
649	
650	- exact source and target concept references and bounded-context identities;
651	- whether the relation imports unchanged meaning, disambiguates a use,
652	  translates directionally, including a specialization, or establishes the
653	  stronger equivalence claim;
654	- direction and any lawful inverse where material;
655	- preserved meaning, changed meaning, loss, and refusal conditions;
656	- source and target semantic owners without transferring either authority;
657	- selected source and target bases, governed scope, and provenance; and
658	- lifecycle and invalidation conditions.
659	
660	A **Semantic Import** adopts the cited meaning unchanged for its declared target
661	scope. A **Semantic Translation** declares how meaning changes in one direction.
662	**Semantic Equivalence** requires the governing authorities to establish the
663	claimed equality; neither identical spelling nor two opposing translations
664	proves it automatically. A **Semantic Disambiguation** selects one meaning for
665	one scope and does not make competing concepts equal. No relation widens its
666	source or target authority.
667	
668	A specialization is a directional translation whose target preserves the
669	declared source meaning while narrowing its admissible instances or adding
670	target-context constraints. It identifies the exact target concept, preserved
671	and narrowed meaning, excluded source instances, and absence or law of any
672	inverse. Calling a term a specialization without those coordinates establishes
673	nothing.

827	
828	Tools discover `stdo_*.json` recursively within the selected workspace
829	boundary. Discovery includes definitions at the workspace root and definitions
830	at arbitrarily deep nested project roots.
831	
832	Directory nesting creates no implicit inheritance, ownership, composition, or
833	constitutional override. Parent and child definitions remain independent until
834	`composition` explicitly relates them. Each composition entry records:
835	
836	- `product_definition` — the current locator for the target definition;
837	- `target_definition_id` — the stable identity expected from the target's
838	  `product.definition_id`;
839	- `relation` — the authority defining the directed composition kind, source
840	  and target roles, owner, scope, lifecycle, and invalidation conditions; and
841	- `contracts` — one or more exact interface, capability, identity, lifecycle,
842	  data, evidence, or other governing contract references consumed by that
843	  relation.
844	
845	Resolution verifies both locator and expected identity. Moving a definition
846	requires a locator update but does not change its identity. Replacing content
847	at the same locator with another definition identity fails closed. When an edge
848	binds exact immutable Product or release versions, the cited relation and
849	contracts also carry and verify those identities; the mutable definition
850	identity cannot substitute for them.

852	A conforming discovered set satisfies all of the following:
853	
854	- every definition validates against its selected released schema;
855	- every required URI and fragment resolves under the declared workspace and
856	  resolver boundary;
857	- every `product.definition_id` is unique;
858	- every build-tenant identity is unique within its Product Definition Overlay;
859	- every governed scope has a resolvable applicable reference-frame basis, and

861	- every local disambiguation binds one exact term, target context, complete
862	  material candidate set, selected concept, authority, basis, and scope, and
863	  `resolves_to` is a member of `disambiguates` and its referenced resolution
864	  carrier is congruent with those bindings;
865	- every material cross-context term seam resolves through an explicit import,
866	  disambiguation, translation, or equivalence relation rather than nominal
867	  match;
868	- every composition target resolves to another product definition whose
869	  `product.definition_id` equals `target_definition_id`, and every relation and
870	  non-empty contract set resolves; and
